name: Manchu flower-bowl platform shoes

lead: Manchu platform shoes (gaodixie) are high-soled shoes worn by Manchu women from the early Qing dynasty into the late Qing. The flowerpot type (huapenxie) has a thick sole that narrows toward the toe and heel, and the horse-hoof type (matixie) stands on a wooden block with concave sides. Both lift the wearer well off the ground.

The visual payoff is extra height and a slender, measured way of walking; the raised block also makes the foot look smaller. Where the style came from is debated, including whether it echoed the gait of Han women with bound feet.

paras: The wooden platform sits under a fabric upper, and the sole was padded with layers of cotton. Left and right shoes were interchangeable. They were worn with Manchu robes and headdress such as the liangbatou.
The shoes are not a modern consumer product, and no health data on them are cited here. Any high platform raises balance and ankle-injury considerations.

lead: Manchu platform shoes were a footwear tradition of Manchu women in the Qing dynasty. The principal type, gaodixie, includes the flowerpot shoe (huapenxie), named for the shape of its sole, and the horse-hoof shoe (matixie), raised on a wooden block with concave sides. [1]

For appearance, the platform adds height and shapes the gait and the look of the foot. The wooden base was topped with a fabric upper and padded with several layers of cotton, and the left and right shoes were interchangeable. [1]

Origin stories include a folk tale of a goddess avoiding mud and insects, a legend of Princess Duoluo Ganzhu whose soldiers used wooden stilts to cross marshes, historians' proposals that the shoes imitated the gait of Han women with bound feet, and the argument that they adapted to conditions in the Northeast. [1]

paras: The flowerpot form has a thick sole narrowing toward toe and heel; the horse-hoof form uses a wooden piece with concave sides; the yuanbaodi style has low heels. The wooden lower part was topped with fabric and the sole was padded with cotton. [1]
The shoes appeared in the early Qing and were still worn in the mid-1800s, when Manchu women's attire combined the platform shoe, the Manchu robe and the liangbatou headdress. [1]

Some historians link the style to the gait of Han Chinese women with bound feet; others reject Han influence as the cause. Late-Qing Manchu women also briefly practiced a loose form of foot binding called liutiaojiao under Han influence. [1]
